The Prevention of Future Deaths reports archive

Lense.ai holds every published Prevention of Future Deaths report in one archive: more than 6,300 reports, together with their responses, updated nightly from the judiciary website. Reading them together shows where the same concerns recur, across years and across coroner areas. The organisations that receive the reports can see every concern in their remit, and whether it recurs. Prevention of Future Deaths reports span healthcare and non-healthcare settings, and the themes and human factors are drawn from every report.

What the tool does

Search

Full-text keyword search

Every report is searchable in full, including reports published as scanned images, which are converted to text.

Search by meaning

Reports are ranked by how closely they match the meaning of the search, so relevant reports are retrieved even where the wording differs: a search for communication failures between teams returns reports concerning handovers, missed referrals and information not passed on.

Filters

Reports can be filtered by category, under either the judiciary or the NHS England category system, by healthcare speciality, and by coroner area, coroner name, NHS region and date of report or date of death, individually or in combination.

Category: Judiciary / NHSHealthcare specialityCoroner areaCoroner nameNHS regionDate

Statistics

Charts of the whole archive, or of a filtered selection

Reports are counted over time and by category — under either the judiciary or the NHS England category system — and by coroner area, coroner name and NHS region. Each chart opens to the underlying reports and can be downloaded as an image or a CSV file.

Trends

Factors and themes are tracked across years, areas and categories, showing whether a concern is becoming more frequent, persisting, or receding.

Downloads

Export

Selected reports can be downloaded together as a ZIP file; the extracted data downloads as an Excel workbook, every value linked to its evidence; charts export as images or CSV, and annotations as CSV.

Analysis

Contributory factors

The Matters of Concern are annotated against the 19 factors of the Yorkshire Contributory Factors Framework. Each annotation is tied to the report sentences that support it.

Recurring themes

Concerns grouped into themes across the whole archive, so the same concern is visible arising in reports written years apart, in different coroner areas.

Facts, sentence-linked

The key facts are recorded from each report, each linked to the sentence that states it: the person who died, with their age, gender, ethnicity and the other Equality Act characteristics where stated; the dates of death, report and publication; the coroner, coroner area and NHS region; the judiciary and NHS categories and the healthcare speciality; the cause of death, the medical condition and drugs; the hospitals named; and the recipients the report was sent to. Where a report does not state a detail, the field remains blank; nothing is assumed.

Automated analysis

Automated, with human review

The tool identifies contributory factors and themes for every report automatically, each linked to its supporting sentences. Any finding can be reviewed — confirmed, rejected or corrected — by a human reviewer; where a finding has been reviewed, the statistics use that decision.

Evaluated

The annotation has been evaluated against expert human annotation on 130 reports, across all 19 factors, with 88% agreement between the tool and the expert reviewers — a substantial level of agreement.

Traceability & audit

Auditable end to end

Every statistic can be traced to the reports behind it, and to the exact sentences within them, so any figure the analysis produces can be verified against the report it came from.

Reports remain at source

The judiciary website remains the authoritative source of each report; the analysis is performed on the text read from it, and every processing step is logged.

Projects

Collaboration between people and organisations

Reports can be grouped into shared projects and supplemented with an organisation’s own reports (a feature disabled by default and enabled on request); a project can be shared with named colleagues within or across organisations, and review progress is tracked across the team.

Search history, tracked and shared

A project keeps the full history of the searches and filters it has been built from, and any past search can be re-opened and run again. New reports collected overnight that match the project’s latest filter are flagged automatically, so the set stays current without any manual refresh. In a shared project the activity log also records which member added or removed reports, and the searches they ran.

Recorded only when stated

The following are taken from the report’s own wording. Where a report does not state them, they remain blank, and therefore absent from the national picture.

  • Date of death a full date
  • Age e.g. “aged 43”
  • Gender from a clear statement
  • Ethnicity when relevant and known
  • Cause of death as listed
  • Disability or condition where stated
  • Drugs named in the report
  • Who it was sent to each party named
  • Hospitals involved named in the report
  • Other protected characteristics pregnancy, religion or belief…
A report is included in each analysis for which it states the detail.

Free to use

Lense.ai is developed and operated for social good by a research group at Loughborough University, supported by a Loughborough University Impact Accelerator Award.

No action is required from any coroner’s office: new reports and responses are collected automatically each night, and the judiciary website remains the authoritative source of every report.
